sections.title: Infection Control, Sterilization, VAP & TB
sections.covers: Transmission-based precautions · cleaning non-disposable equipment · sterilization processes · VAP and how to reduce it · tuberculosis

q.q: What is the single best way to prevent transmission of hospital-acquired infections?
o: Wearing an N95 at all times
q.e: Most hospital-acquired infections come from direct contact between patients and healthcare workers, so hand hygiene is the single best prevention.

q.q: Transmission-based precautions are used:
o: Only for patients in the ICU
q.e: Transmission-based precautions are always layered on top of standard precautions, never instead of them.

q.q: Droplet transmission involves particles of what size, traveling about how far?
o: Larger than 5 μm; about 3 feet or less
Larger than 5 μm; up to 25 feet
5 μm or smaller; about 3 feet or less
q.e: Droplets > 5 μm fall out fast and travel ≤ 3 feet. Airborne droplet nuclei ≤ 5 μm stay suspended and can travel long distances.

q.q: Which diseases require AIRBORNE precautions?
q.e: Airborne: TB, measles (rubeola), chickenpox, Aspergillus, smallpox, SARS. Influenza/pertussis/mumps/meningitis are droplet; MRSA/C. diff are contact.

q.q: Which diseases require DROPLET precautions?
o: MRSA, C. difficile, and wound infections
q.e: Droplet: bacterial meningitis, pertussis, influenza, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, group A strep, epiglottitis (H. influenzae), SARS.

q.q: A patient has C. difficile diarrhea. Which precautions are required?
q.e: Contact: GI infections (C. diff, norovirus), wound/skin infections, MRSA. Gloves and gown on entering the room.

q.q: Which precautions does the deck assign to RSV?
q.e: The deck lists RSV as contact + droplet together.

q.q: What room is required for a patient on AIRBORNE precautions?
o: Private room with normal airflow, door open
Semi-private room with a curtain drawn
q.e: Negative pressure pulls air into the room so contaminated air can't escape. Droplet patients need a private room but no special air handling.

q.q: What respiratory protection must the RT wear for a patient on airborne precautions?
o: A fit-tested N95, seal-checked each time
A surgical mask plus a gown
No mask unless suctioning the patient
q.e: Fit-tested NIOSH N95 (user-seal check every time), or a PAPR for poor fit or highest protection. The patient wears a surgical mask for transport.

q.q: When caring for a patient on droplet precautions, when must the RT wear a surgical mask?
o: When within 3 feet of the patient
Only when the patient is coughing
q.e: Droplet: surgical mask within 3 feet; eye protection for aerosol-generating procedures; patient masked for transport.

q.q: What is the correct order for PUTTING ON PPE?
o: Hair/foot covers → gown → mask → goggles → gloves
Gloves → gown → mask → goggles → hair/foot covers
Mask → gloves → gown → goggles → hair/foot covers
Gown → gloves → goggles → mask → hair/foot covers
q.e: Heuer Table 7-3. Removing: hair/foot covers → goggles → mask → gloves → gown.

q.q: What is the correct order for REMOVING PPE per Heuer?
o: Hair/foot covers → goggles → mask → gloves → gown
Gloves → gown → mask → goggles → hair/foot covers
Gown → gloves → mask → goggles → hair/foot covers
Mask → goggles → gown → gloves → hair/foot covers
q.e: Removing (Heuer): hair/foot → goggles/face shield → mask → gloves (peel inside out) → gown (inside out).

q.q: Aerosolized pentamidine must be given in a negative-pressure room with how many air changes per hour?
q.e: The deck: 6 air changes per hour, or a booth/hood with a HEPA-filtered exhaust. This is the pentamidine-specific figure.

q.q: Why must equipment be CLEANED before it is disinfected or sterilized?
o: Organic debris shields organisms from the disinfecting agent
Cleaning kills all spores on its own
Disinfectants only work on wet surfaces
Cleaning is optional for semicritical items
q.e: Cleaning physically removes foreign material. An item that has not been cleaned cannot be reliably disinfected or sterilized.

q.q: Items that enter the bloodstream or sterile body areas (surgical instruments, bronchoscope forceps) are classified as:
q.e: Spaulding: critical → sterilization; semicritical → sterilization or high-level disinfection; noncritical → washing or low/intermediate disinfection.

q.q: Ventilator circuits, bronchoscopes, laryngoscope blades and nondisposable nebulizers are classified as:
q.e: They contact intact mucous membranes. Most respiratory care equipment is semicritical, so high-level disinfection is the RT's everyday standard.

q.q: A stethoscope and a blood pressure cuff are classified as:
q.e: Noncritical items touch only intact skin. Stethoscopes: wipe with 70% alcohol, kept wet ≥ 10 seconds.

q.q: After immersion in a liquid disinfectant, semicritical equipment should be rinsed with:
q.e: Rinse with sterile water. If not feasible: filtered or tap water, then an isopropyl alcohol rinse and forced-air drying.

q.q: How often should in-use ventilator circuits be changed, per Heuer/CDC/AARC?
o: Only when visibly soiled or malfunctioning
Routinely every 24 hours on a schedule
Routinely every 48 hours on a schedule
Routinely every 7 days on a schedule
q.e: Routine changes increase contamination. (One deck slide says every 7 days, but its own notes and Heuer/CDC/AARC say not routinely.)

q.q: Humidifiers on ventilator circuits should be filled with:
o: Distilled tap water from the unit
q.e: Fill humidifiers with sterile water only.

q.q: How should a small-volume nebulizer be handled between treatments on the same patient?
o: Clean, rinse with sterile water, and air dry
Discard and replace after each treatment
Leave the leftover medication in the cup
q.e: Between treatments on the same patient: clean, rinse with sterile water, air dry.

q.q: Which process destroys ALL forms of microbial life, including spores?
q.e: High-level disinfection kills vegetative bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi and viruses but not necessarily spores.

q.q: How is a heat-SENSITIVE critical item sterilized?
o: Ethylene oxide gas or H₂O₂ vapor
q.e: Heat-tolerant critical items → steam autoclave. Heat-sensitive → EtO, H₂O₂ vapor, or a liquid chemical sterilant.

q.q: How is a heat-TOLERANT critical item sterilized?
q.e: Steam autoclave = moist heat sterilization for heat-tolerant critical items.

q.q: Glutaraldehyde (Cidex) provides high-level disinfection in ______ and sterilization in ______.
q.e: Glutaraldehyde: HLD in 20 minutes at room temperature; true sterilization takes a full 10 hours.

q.q: Pasteurization of respiratory equipment uses:
q.e: Pasteurization = high-level disinfection (not sterilization) for heat-sensitive semicritical items like circuits and humidifiers.

q.q: Is pasteurization a sterilization method?
q.e: Pasteurization is high-level disinfection, not sterilization.

q.q: Which is the BEST method for verifying that a sterilization cycle worked?
q.e: Biological indicators test whether spores were killed. Include them in every cycle with critical items, otherwise at least weekly.

q.q: A chemical indicator on a sterilized package has not changed color. What should the RT do?
o: Use it — the cycle log was normal
Wipe it with alcohol and use it
Re-seal it and use it within 24 hours
q.e: Chemical indicators change color when the correct temperature or gas concentration is reached. No change = get a replacement.

q.q: What bleach dilution is used for routine surfaces during a C. difficile outbreak or a large blood spill?
q.e: 1:10 for C. diff surfaces and large spills; 1:100 for small spills (< 10 mL); 1:50 for 5 minutes for home semicritical items.

q.q: What skin prep is used before central line insertion (CDC bundle)?
o: Soap and water, rinsed and dried
q.e: Chlorhexidine 2% in 70% isopropyl alcohol scrubbed into the site for 30 seconds.

q.q: How is VAP defined for exam purposes?
o: Pneumonia ≥ 48 hours after intubation, not present on admission
Pneumonia that appears within the first 24 hours of intubation
Any pneumonia at all in a patient on a ventilator
Pneumonia that first appears after the patient is extubated
q.e: Safest answer: 48 hours or more after intubation, in a patient not admitted with pneumonia. (The deck says 48–72 hours.)

q.q: What is the PRIMARY mechanism of VAP?
o: Microaspiration of secretions pooled above the cuff
Contamination of the wall oxygen supply
Airborne spread from other ICU patients
Blood-borne spread from infected IV lines
q.e: The ETT bypasses upper-airway defenses and secretions leak past the cuff. The single greatest risk factor is prolonged ventilation.

q.q: VAP affects what percentage of ventilated patients?
q.e: VAP affects 10–25% of ventilated patients, ~25% of ICU infections, with mortality 33–50%.

q.q: Which findings raise suspicion of VAP?
o: New infiltrates plus fever, high WBC, purulent sputum
Clear chest x-ray with a low-grade fever
Improving compliance and a falling PIP
Normal WBC with thin, white secretions
q.e: New or progressive infiltrates plus clinical signs. Confirmation requires a lower respiratory tract culture obtained before starting antibiotics.

q.q: To what angle should the head of the bed be elevated to prevent VAP?
q.e: HOB 30–45° unless contraindicated (e.g., after neurosurgery, severe hypotension).

q.q: Which is part of the VAP prevention bundle?
o: Daily sedation vacation with a spontaneous breathing trial
Changing the ventilator circuit every 24 hours
q.e: Bundle: HOB 30–45°, sedation vacation + SBT, peptic ulcer prophylaxis, DVT prophylaxis, chlorhexidine oral care, subglottic ETT, closed suction.

q.q: Which agent is used for daily oral care to prevent VAP?
q.e: Daily oral care with chlorhexidine, plus brushing teeth, rotating the ETT position every 24 hours, and moisturizer.

q.q: Which suction system does the AARC endorse to reduce VAP?
o: Open suction with a new catheter every pass
q.e: Closed suction means the circuit is never broken.

q.q: Which route of intubation reduces VAP risk?
q.e: Use the oral route; nasal intubation causes sinusitis and more VAP. Avoid intubation entirely with NIV where possible.

q.q: According to the deck, what is the single best way to prevent VAP?
q.e: Extubate as early as it is safe. Remember: cuff 20–30 cm H₂O, HOB 30–45°, wash hands, extubate early.

q.q: A patient has been ventilated for 10 days and develops VAP. Which organisms are most likely?
q.e: First 48 hr: H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae. 3–7 days: gram-negative bacilli. > 7 days: resistant organisms including MRSA.

q.q: Why is TB classically an UPPER-lobe disease?
o: It is aerobic and thrives where O₂ tension is highest
The upper lobes receive the most blood flow
Gravity carries the bacilli to the apices
The lower lobes have more macrophages to kill it
q.e: Aerobic bacillus → lung apices. Its waxy capsule resists disinfectants and needs acid-fast staining.

q.q: Why must a bronchoscope used on a TB patient be sterilized rather than just disinfected?
o: Its waxy capsule resists many disinfectants
TB is spread only through the blood
q.e: The waxy capsule resists disinfectants, so TB/hepatitis B exposure escalates a scope to sterilization.

q.q: How is TB transmitted?
o: Airborne droplet nuclei from coughs and sneezes
Direct skin-to-skin contact with the patient
Blood transfusion from an infected donor
q.e: Droplet nuclei (0.5–1.0 μm) stay airborne for hours — hence airborne precautions.

q.q: Which statement about LATENT TB is correct?
o: Walled off, asymptomatic, and not infectious
Active disease that is highly contagious
The same thing as miliary TB
q.e: Latent: sealed in tubercles, dormant, asymptomatic, not infectious. Reactivation TB is highly infectious.

q.q: Which set of symptoms suggests REACTIVATION (active) TB?
o: Low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss, bloody sputum
High fever, inspiratory stridor, drooling, and tripod position
Wheezing that fully reverses after a dose of albuterol
Pink frothy sputum with orthopnea and leg edema
q.e: Reactivation: low-grade fever, fatigue, night sweats, violent cough, green or bloody sputum, chest pain, anorexia, weight loss.

q.q: Which test is recommended to diagnose LATENT TB infection?
q.e: Heuer: skin test for latent TB; serial sputum AFB for active TB; CXR and IGRA added to confirm.

q.q: When is a Mantoux (PPD) skin test read?
q.e: Read the induration at 48–72 hours.

q.q: Using the deck's thresholds, a PPD induration of 12 mm is:
q.e: Deck: < 5 mm negative; 5–9 mm suspicious; ≥ 10 mm positive. Positive means exposure or latent TB, not necessarily active disease.

q.q: How many sputum samples are collected for AFB testing?
q.e: 3 samples over 8–24 hours, each ≥ 5 mL of deep lung secretions; saliva is not acceptable.

q.q: What solution is used for sputum induction?
o: Normal saline instilled into the airway
q.e: Hypertonic saline via ultrasonic or continuous jet nebulizer for 15–20 min, in a negative-pressure room with the RT in an N95.

q.q: During sputum induction, the FEV₁ falls 22% from baseline. What should the RT do?
q.e: Stop if FEV₁ falls ≥ 20%. Pretreat reactive-airway patients with a fast-acting β-agonist.

q.q: Which chest x-ray finding is classic for advanced TB?
q.e: Upper-lobe/apical disease: Ghon nodule early, cavitation in advanced disease, calcification and fibrosis when chronic; miliary = tiny nodules throughout.

q.q: What is the induction phase of the 6-month TB regimen?
o: INH, RIF, PZA and EMB for 2 months
RIF and INH for 6 months only
PZA and EMB for 4 months only
q.e: Induction 2 months INH + RIF + PZA + EMB/SM; continuation 4 months INH + RIF. INH alone for 1 year is prophylaxis.

q.q: How is multidrug-resistant TB from noncompliance countered?
q.e: DOT: a healthcare worker watches each dose. Once resistance is documented, add ≥ 3 more antibiotics and extend the course.

sections.title: Medical Gas Delivery, Cylinders & Flow Devices
sections.covers: Cylinders · LOX and gaseous systems · cylinder factors and duration · concentrators · home delivery devices · flow and delivered O₂ · condensate · air-entrainment · NRB · Briggs adaptor · Bourdon vs Thorpe

q.q: What is the standard working pressure of piped hospital O₂ and air?
q.e: Piped wall gas runs at 50 psi — what ventilators, blenders and flowmeters are built for.

q.q: A full O₂ cylinder is assumed to be at what pressure for duration calculations?
q.e: Heuer's table assumes 2200 psi, but filling pressures vary — always check the gauge first.

q.q: Which safety system is used on the yoke of small cylinders (e.g., E cylinders)?
q.e: PISS = small-cylinder yoke. DISS = threaded connection off 50-psi piped sources (ventilators, blenders, suction).

q.q: A small cylinder with a PISS regulator is hissing. What is the most likely cause?
o: A loose connection or a bad washer
The flowmeter is set too high
q.e: Hissing = loose connection or missing/damaged washer. Tighten the regulator or replace the washer.

q.q: After opening a cylinder valve fully, what should the RT do?
o: Turn it back half a turn
q.e: Open slowly all the way, then back half a turn so the valve doesn't "freeze" fully open.

q.q: When should an O₂ cylinder be changed out per Heuer?
q.e: Change out 15–30 minutes before empty, or when below 500 psi.

q.q: How should a large cylinder be transported?
o: Laid flat on the patient's bed
q.e: Large cylinders go chained to a wheeled cart; small ones in the gurney or wheelchair holder.

q.q: Which O₂ cylinder may be taken into the MRI suite?
o: Any cylinder if it is full
A steel cylinder with a brass regulator
q.e: Iron-free equipment only — the magnet can turn a steel cylinder into a projectile.

q.q: For a transport with a possible delay, how much O₂ should be carried?
o: At least twice the volume needed for a one-way trip
Exactly the volume for a one-way trip
q.e: The transport deck: an E cylinder must be full, and carry at least twice the one-way volume.

q.q: What is the duration-of-flow formula for a gas cylinder?
q.e: Duration (min) = (psig × factor) ÷ L/min.

q.q: What is the cylinder factor for an E cylinder?
q.e: D 0.16, E 0.28, G 2.41 (Heuer also prints 2.14), H/K 3.14.

q.q: What is the cylinder factor for an H or K cylinder?
What is the cylinder factor for a D cylinder?
An E cylinder reads 800 psi and is running at 5 L/min. How long until it is empty?
A full E cylinder (2200 psi) runs at 3 L/min. Using the 500-psi change-out rule, how long until it must be changed?
An H cylinder reads 1800 psi and the patient needs 6 L/min. How long will it last?
A D cylinder reads 1000 psi at 2 L/min. How long will it last?
An E cylinder reads 1500 psi at 4 L/min. How long will it last?
As a ballpark, how long does a full E cylinder last at 10 L/min?
q.e: Full E at 10 L/min ≈ 1 hr; full H at 10 L/min ≈ 10 hr.

q.q: 1 liter of liquid oxygen vaporizes into about how many liters of gas?
q.e: 1 L liquid = 860 L gas; 1 lb LOX ≈ 344 L gas.

q.q: 1 pound of liquid oxygen yields about how many liters of gaseous O₂?
q.e: Gaseous O₂ (L) = LOX weight (lb) × 344.

q.q: A home LOX base unit holds 75 lb and runs at 2 L/min continuously. About how long will it last?
A LOX reservoir holds 50 lb, running at 2 L/min. About how long will it last?
A patient's stationary LOX tank makes an occasional, intermittent hissing sound. What should the RT tell the patient?
o: This is normal venting — keep the tank upright
Switch to backup O₂ and call the supplier
q.e: Intermittent hissing is normal. Loud, constant hissing with visible mist is a problem → backup O₂, call supplier.

q.q: A LOX tank makes loud, constant hissing with a steady stream of mist. What should be done?
o: Switch to backup O₂ and call the supplier
Lay the tank on its side to stop venting
Increase the flow rate to use the gas up
q.e: Loud constant hissing + mist is a malfunction.

q.q: How long does a typical full portable LOX unit last with a demand-flow device?
q.e: ~1 L LOX, < 6 lb, 8+ hours with a conserving device.

q.q: How does an oxygen concentrator produce O₂?
o: A sieve adsorbs nitrogen from room air
It splits water into H₂ and O₂
It compresses room air to 2200 psi
q.e: The sieve adsorbs nitrogen, CO₂ and water vapor, letting O₂ pass through.

q.q: What O₂ concentration does a concentrator produce?
o: About 21%, the same as room air
q.e: 90–95% up to 10 L/min. Higher flow = less contact time with the sieve.

q.q: A concentrator's analyzed output is below 85–90% of the manufacturer's spec. What is the cause and action?
o: Exhausted sieve — use backup, replace the unit
Dirty intake filter — clean it and continue
Flow set too low — increase it and recheck
Normal for concentrators — no action needed
q.e: Exhausted sodium-aluminum pellets → gaseous backup and replace/service the concentrator.

q.q: A concentrator alarm sounds. What is the first thing to check?
q.e: Clean the intake filters and keep the unit away from walls and curtains.

q.q: A patient using a concentrator at 4 L/min by cannula complains of nasal dryness. What should the RT do?
q.e: At ≥ 4 L/min, add a bubble humidifier for nasal dryness.

q.q: Most portable oxygen concentrators deliver pulse-dose only. What is their limit?
q.e: Pulse-dose POCs suit patients needing ≤ 30% O₂; only continuous-flow units exceed 30%.

q.q: For air travel with a POC, how much battery should the patient carry?
o: At least 150% of the one-way travel time
q.e: Airlines aren't required to supply electricity or oxygen; carry battery for ≥ 150% of one-way travel.

q.q: Which home O₂ system is the most cost-efficient for continuous low-flow O₂?
q.e: Concentrators are the most cost-efficient for continuous low-flow; they never run out while powered.

q.q: A patient with restricted activity needs home O₂. What system should the RT recommend?
o: A portable LOX unit by itself
q.e: Restricted activity → concentrator + backup cylinder. Ambulatory → always add a portable source.

q.q: An active, ambulatory home O₂ patient needs extended flow duration. What should be added?
q.e: Conserving devices cut O₂ use by 50–75%, doubling or tripling duration.

q.q: By how much do O₂-conserving devices reduce O₂ usage?
q.e: 50–75%, doubling or tripling duration of flow from any source.

q.q: A patient uses O₂ only during sleep. What system is sufficient?
q.e: Sleep-only users don't need a portable source.

q.q: A demand-flow device fails. What continuous flow should be used as a backup?
q.e: If the conserving device fails, switch to continuous O₂ at 2–3× the conserving-device flow.

q.q: What are the Medicare qualifying criteria for home O₂ at rest?
q.e: For a hospitalized patient, the value must be obtained no sooner than 48 hours before discharge.

q.q: On a nasal cannula, each 1 L/min adds roughly how much to the FiO₂?
Approximately what FiO₂ does a nasal cannula at 3 L/min deliver?
On a low-flow device, which patient change LOWERS the delivered FiO₂?
o: Faster rate and larger tidal volume
q.e: Higher inspiratory flow, VT, rate or minute ventilation → more room-air dilution → lower FiO₂.

q.q: Why are low-flow devices ordered in L/min rather than as an FiO₂?
o: FiO₂ cannot be measured at all
q.e: Low-flow gas is less than the patient's inspiratory flow, so it is diluted with room air — FiO₂ is variable.

q.q: On a high-flow air-entrainment device, how should oxygenation be adjusted?
o: Change the FiO₂, not the flow
Change the flow, not the FiO₂
q.e: Turning the flow down doesn't change FiO₂ but may fail to meet demand, making FiO₂ variable again.

q.q: Aerosol tubing is completely filled with water and there is no gurgling sound. What should the RT do?
o: Drain the tubing and add a water trap
q.e: Tubing blocked by condensate → drain and add a water trap at low points.

q.q: The analyzed O₂% on an air-entrainment nebulizer is HIGHER than set. What is the likely cause?
o: A leak at the humidifier jar
q.e: Back pressure acts like a partially obstructed entrainment port → less air entrained → higher O₂%. Drain and add a water trap.

q.q: Why does condensate (rainout) form in heated circuits?
o: Saturated gas cools along the tubing
The patient exhales too much water
The set gas flow is too low
q.e: Fixes: heated-wire circuit, inline water trap, or an HME for temporary use.

q.q: In an air-entrainment device, what happens when the entrainment port is made LARGER?
o: Lower FiO₂ and higher total flow
Higher FiO₂ and higher total flow
Higher FiO₂ and lower total flow
Lower FiO₂ and lower total flow
q.e: Bigger ports / smaller jets → more air → lower FiO₂, higher total flow.

q.q: What is the air-to-O₂ ratio for 40% O₂?
What is the air-to-O₂ ratio for 60% O₂?
q.e: 60% is the pivot at 1:1. Below 60% the ratio is > 1:1; above 60% it is < 1:1.

q.q: What is the air-to-O₂ ratio for 28% O₂?
A 35% air-entrainment mask is set at 8 L/min. What is the total flow?
q.e: 35% = 5:1 → 6 total parts × 8 = 48 L/min (Heuer B.27/B.28).

q.q: A 40% air-entrainment mask is set at 8 L/min. Does it meet a 40 L/min inspiratory demand?
q.e: 40% = 3:1 → 4 parts × 8 = 32 L/min < 40. Raise input to 12 L/min → 48 L/min.

q.q: A 28% Venturi mask runs at 4 L/min. What is the total flow?
What total flow does Heuer say ensures a stable FiO₂?
q.e: "The best way to ensure a stable FIO₂ is to provide a total flow of at least 40 L/min."

q.q: A patient needs 70% O₂ with a high inspiratory flow demand. Which is the best approach?
o: A blender system or heated HFNC
q.e: At 70%, 15 × 1.6 = 24 L/min — entrainment fails. Above 0.60 at > 40 L/min, use a blender system or HFNC.

q.q: Raising the O₂ input flow on an air-entrainment device changes:
o: The total flow, not the FiO₂
The FiO₂, not the total flow
q.e: The ratio (and FiO₂) is set by the port/jet; input flow changes total flow.

q.q: What is the minimum flow for a nonrebreather mask?
o: 10 L/min — enough to keep the bag up
6 L/min — same as a simple mask
q.e: Minimum 10 L/min — the flow that keeps the reservoir bag from collapsing.

q.q: What FiO₂ does a nonrebreather deliver per Heuer?
q.e: Heuer Table 6-1: 60–80%. It is a low-flow/variable-performance reservoir device.

q.q: The NRB reservoir bag collapses when the patient inhales. What should the RT do?
q.e: A collapsing bag = flow too low or minute ventilation increased — turn it up.

q.q: The NRB bag stays fully inflated during inhalation. What is the first likely cause?
q.e: Too much flow → decrease until the bag deflates slightly on inspiration. If flow is right: large mask leak, then a jammed/reversed valve.

q.q: A physician orders an NRB for a patient in respiratory arrest. What should the RT recommend?
q.e: An NRB does not provide ventilation. Recommend a BVM that can give 100% O₂ and ventilate.

q.q: A patient's SpO₂ rises only from 83% to 87% when switched from a simple mask to an NRB. What should the RT recommend?
o: HFNC at 20–40 L/min or mask CPAP
q.e: The patient can't meet high inspiratory demand or is shunting. HFNC titrated to SpO₂, or mask CPAP.

q.q: What happens if the valves are removed from a nonrebreather?
o: It becomes a partial rebreathing mask
It becomes a simple mask with no bag
q.e: Hess: removing the valves converts the NRB to a partial rebreather (6–10 L/min, 40–70%).

q.q: What is a Briggs adaptor?
o: A T-piece joining aerosol tubing to an airway
A valve that adds PEEP to a circuit
A regulator for small O₂ cylinders
A type of high-flow nasal cannula
q.e: The T-piece (Briggs adapter) is an LVN interface: inspiratory limb in, stem to the airway, expiratory arm open.

q.q: Why is reservoir tubing added to the expiratory limb of a Briggs adaptor?
o: So the patient draws source gas instead of room air
To increase the O₂ percentage above the set value
q.e: It keeps the FiO₂ stable when the patient's demand exceeds the nebulizer output.

q.q: On a T-piece, the aerosol mist disappears during inspiration. What does this mean?
o: The FiO₂ is set too high
q.e: Fix: maximize input flow, add expiratory reservoir tubing, or run nebulizers in parallel.

q.q: How is a T-piece used during weaning?
o: For an SBT with no ventilator support
To deliver 10 cm H₂O of PEEP
q.e: A T-piece SBT gives no assistance; the patient does all the work, typically for 30 minutes.

q.q: Why is a Bourdon gauge used on transport cylinders instead of a Thorpe tube?
o: It is not affected by gravity
It is more accurate with back pressure
q.e: A Thorpe tube floats a ball in a vertical tube and must stay upright; a Bourdon gauge reads the same at any angle.

q.q: A Bourdon gauge's outlet becomes completely obstructed. What does the gauge show?
q.e: A Bourdon gauge is a pressure gauge calibrated in L/min; back pressure makes it over-read. A fully obstructed Bourdon still reads flow.

q.q: Which flowmeter shows the ACTUAL outlet flow regardless of downstream resistance?
q.e: A pressure-compensated Thorpe tube displays actual flow regardless of downstream resistance.

q.q: How should the accuracy of an O₂ blender be checked?
o: Check it with a calibrated O₂ analyzer
Trust the dial setting on the blender
q.e: Verify with a second instrument. If off, check both source pressures and leaks, then replace the blender.

q.q: 80/20 heliox is run through an O₂ flowmeter set at 10 L/min. What is the actual flow?
70/30 heliox is run through an O₂ flowmeter set at 8 L/min. What is the actual flow?

q.q: When should a patient prime an MDI?
o: When new or unused for a few days
Only when the canister is cold
q.e: Shake and prime (waste a dose into the air) if new or unused for a few days. Warm a cold canister in the hands.

q.q: Using the open-mouth MDI technique, how far from the mouth should the MDI be held?
q.e: Open-mouth: 2 inches away with the tongue down, which enhances lung deposition.

q.q: When should the patient actuate the MDI?
o: At the start of a slow, deep breath
At the very end of inhalation
q.e: Actuate at the start of a slow, deep 3–5 second inhalation — not before, not after.

q.q: How long should the patient hold the breath after an MDI puff?
q.e: A 10-second breath-hold allows maximum deposition (gravitational settling).

q.q: How long should the patient wait between MDI puffs?
q.e: Wait about 1 minute between puffs.

q.q: Why must a patient rinse and spit after using a steroid MDI?
o: To prevent thrush and reduce absorption
To remove the propellant taste only
To rinse the MDI mouthpiece clean
To speed up the drug's onset
q.e: Rinse and spit prevents pharyngitis and thrush and reduces the drug swallowed.

q.q: How should the RT confirm the patient learned MDI technique?
o: Watch the patient take the first home dose
q.e: Confirm learning with a return demonstration: "Show me how you'll use your inhaler at home."

q.q: An adult who is not acutely ill cannot coordinate MDI actuation with breathing. What should the RT recommend?
o: Add a valved holding chamber (or a breath-actuated MDI)
Switch to a DPI with a spacer
Stop the MDI and use oral medication
Tell the patient to actuate twice per breath
q.e: Heuer: add a holding chamber; a breath-actuated MDI is the alternative.

q.q: What is the main advantage of a spacer or valved holding chamber?
o: A faster onset of drug action
A higher dose delivered per puff
No need to rinse after steroids
q.e: The propellant dries and large particles fall out — less throat deposition and less thrush with steroids.

q.q: How does a valved holding chamber differ from a plain spacer?
o: A one-way valve holds the aerosol until inhalation
It has no valve and requires perfect timing
It is designed for use with DPIs only
It turns the MDI dose into a nebulized mist
q.e: The valve stops the patient from exhaling into the chamber and gives a bit more deposition. VHCs are preferred.

q.q: How many MDI puffs should be actuated into a holding chamber per inhalation?
o: As many as prescribed at once
q.e: Actuate only once per inhalation — never stack puffs into the chamber.

q.q: A small child uses an MDI with a holding chamber and face mask. How many breaths per actuation?
q.e: With a mask, 3–5 breaths per actuation. The mask cuts lung deposition by 50% — wean to a mouthpiece when possible.

q.q: How should a plastic valved holding chamber be cleaned?
o: Monthly in dilute detergent, then air-dried
q.e: Air-dry; hand-drying builds an electrostatic charge that pulls drug onto the walls.

q.q: Which device must NEVER be used with a spacer or holding chamber?
q.e: DPIs, breath-actuated MDIs and Respimat cannot be used with a spacer or VHC.

q.q: The pMDI is the method of choice for children under 5 years old ONLY when:
o: It is used with a spacer or valved holding chamber
The child can hold the breath 10 seconds
It is used without a mask
q.e: Under 5 years: pMDI only with a reservoir device.

q.q: How does a dry-powder inhaler work?
o: The patient's inspiratory flow disperses it
A propellant sprays the drug out
A vibrating mesh creates a mist
q.e: DPIs are breath-actuated — no propellant, no timing problem, but they need a high inspiratory flow.

q.q: What inspiratory flow does a DPI require (Heuer Ch 12)?
o: A rapid, deep inhalation of about 60 L/min
A slow inhalation of about 10 L/min
A 3–5 second slow inhalation at 30 L/min
q.e: Heuer: rapid, deep inhalation at 60 L/min (the deck says 30–90 L/min). Children under 4 usually can't generate it.

q.q: Which instruction about DPIs is correct?
o: Never exhale into the device after loading it
Rinse the device in water after each use
Use it with a spacer for better deposition
q.e: Exhaling into it loses the dose and cakes the powder. Keep it dry; never use with a spacer.

q.q: An acutely ill adult cannot use an MDI or DPI. Which device is the fallback?
q.e: The SVN needs the least coordination — slow tidal breathing with occasional deep breaths, any age.

q.q: What gas flow should power a small-volume jet nebulizer?
q.e: 6–8 L/min produces the optimal 1–5 μm particle size.

q.q: Why is a mouthpiece preferred over a face mask for SVN treatments?
o: A face mask cuts lung deposition by about 50%
A mouthpiece increases the drug dose
A face mask cannot be used with oxygen
q.e: Mask use halves lung deposition. Avoid "blow-by" in infants.

q.q: Which nebulizer should be avoided for suspensions because its crystal's heat can degrade some drugs?
q.e: The USN's piezoelectric crystal generates heat; not for suspensions.

q.q: Which nebulizer is preferred for mechanically ventilated patients and adds no gas flow to the circuit?
q.e: Vibrating mesh: electric, no propellant or compressor, uniform fine mist, preferred in-line.

q.q: Which device is used to deliver aerosolized ribavirin for RSV?
q.e: The Small Particle Aerosol Generator (≈1.3 μm). Replace the reservoir solution every 24 hours.

q.q: What particle size range is the bronchoactive target for bronchodilators?
q.e: > 10 μm → upper airway; 5–10 μm → upper airway/first generations; 2–5 μm → lower respiratory tract; < 1 μm largely exhaled.

q.q: Where do aerosol particles larger than 10 μm deposit?
q.e: Particles > 10 μm deposit in the upper airway.

q.q: What MMAD is recommended for pentamidine to maximize alveolar deposition?
q.e: 1–2 μm for pentamidine.

q.q: Which deposition mechanism does the 10-second breath-hold take advantage of?
q.e: Sedimentation depends on particle size and time. Inertial impaction occurs in large, fast-flow airways; diffusion dominates < 1 μm.

q.q: A spacer and slow inhalation are designed to reduce which deposition mechanism?
q.e: Inertial impaction depends on mass and velocity; it happens where flow is fastest.

q.q: What is the mechanism of incentive spirometry?
o: A slow, held maximal breath that reopens alveoli
Positive pressure delivered by a machine
q.e: A slow inspiration to near TLC, held, raises transpulmonary pressure and restores FRC.

q.q: What is the main indication for incentive spirometry?
o: Treating atelectasis in a cooperative patient
Removing thick secretions in cystic fibrosis
q.e: Heuer: IS is no longer recommended for routine post-op prophylaxis — early mobilization is primary. It remains appropriate for documented or suspected atelectasis.

q.q: What minimum inspiratory capacity should a patient generate to use IS effectively?
q.e: If the patient can't cooperate or generate IC > 33% of predicted, recommend IPPB or intermittent CPAP.

q.q: A post-op patient cannot cooperate with incentive spirometry. What should the RT recommend?
q.e: Escalate per the Lung Expansion Therapy Protocol.

q.q: How long should the patient hold the breath at the end of an IS inspiration?
q.e: Inhale slowly to full IC, hold 5–10 seconds, exhale, then rest.

q.q: How often should incentive spirometry be performed?
q.e: 6–10 SMIs per hour while awake (the deck teaches ~10 breaths hourly).

q.q: When should the RT teach incentive spirometry to a surgical patient?
o: Pre-op, to set the post-op target
Only after the first post-op day
Only if atelectasis shows on x-ray
q.e: Teach preoperatively; the deck's target is at least half the pre-op IC.

q.q: What is the most common reason incentive spirometry fails?
q.e: Pain is the primary hazard — medicate and splint the incision.

q.q: A patient becomes dizzy with tingling fingers during IS. What should the RT do?
q.e: Breaths are too frequent → hyperventilation. Allow adequate recovery time.

q.q: A patient is blowing into the incentive spirometer instead of inhaling. What should the RT do?
o: Replace the device with a new one
Switch the patient to PEP therapy
q.e: Blowing into the indicator is the classic error — the patient must inhale through it.

q.q: When can incentive spirometry be discontinued per Heuer?
o: After 24 hours, regardless of volume achieved
When the patient reaches 500 mL once
q.e: Discontinue at > 60–70% predicted IC with improved breath sounds, oxygenation and respiratory rate.

q.q: How does PEP therapy help clear secretions?
o: Back-pressure splints airways and gets air behind mucus
It creates positive pressure during inspiration
It vibrates the chest wall from the outside
It chemically thins mucus in the airways
q.e: PEP prevents premature airway closure and uses collateral channels to push secretions proximally.

q.q: What is the therapeutic PEP working range?
q.e: Devices generate 6–25 cm H₂O; start at the lowest setting and titrate to 10–20 cm H₂O.

q.q: How should PEP exhalation be performed?
o: Passively, with no effort at all
q.e: Sets of 10–20 breaths with active, not forced, exhalation; then huff cough. Repeat 4–8 cycles, ≤ 20 minutes.

q.q: After each set of 10–20 PEP breaths, the patient should:
q.e: The forced expiratory technique: 2–3 huffs with the glottis open, then rest.

q.q: Which condition is a contraindication to PEP therapy?
q.e: Also: hemodynamic instability, bullous emphysema, ↑ ICP, sinusitis, epistaxis, middle-ear problems.

q.q: How does PEP differ from PEEP?
o: PEP: exhaled resistance, spontaneous patient; PEEP: vent baseline
PEP and PEEP are two names for the same therapy
PEP acts on inspiration; PEEP acts only on exhalation
PEP is used only on ventilated, intubated patients
q.e: PEP = handheld, exhalation only, returns to zero, for airway clearance. PEEP = machine baseline, never returns to zero, for oxygenation.

q.q: Which vibratory PEP device is gravity-dependent and must be held at the correct angle?
q.e: The Flutter's steel ball is gravity-dependent. The Acapella works in any position and accepts a nebulizer.

q.q: At what frequency do vibratory PEP devices oscillate?
q.e: Vibratory PEP (Flutter, Acapella, Aerobika) oscillates at 10–30 Hz.

q.q: A PEP device generates no pressure. What is the most likely cause?
o: A leak at a connection or the mouth seal
The patient is exhaling too slowly
q.e: No pressure = leak. Unexpectedly HIGH pressure = obstructed outlet port (hand or bedding).

q.q: How does the RT confirm a vibratory PEP device is set correctly?
q.e: If you can't feel the vibrations, the settings are wrong.

q.q: How does cromolyn sodium work?
q.e: Cromolyn (Intal) is a mast cell stabilizer with no bronchodilator activity.

q.q: A patient in an acute asthma attack asks to use cromolyn. What should the RT do?
o: Give a SABA — cromolyn is preventive only
q.e: Cromolyn cannot reverse bronchoconstriction that has already happened. In an attack, give albuterol.

q.q: How long does cromolyn take to improve symptoms?
q.e: Tell the patient to keep taking it even though nothing seems to happen at first.

q.q: What is the SVN dose of cromolyn sodium?
q.e: SVN 20 mg/2 mL (1%) QID. MDI 1 mg/puff, 2–4 puffs QID.

q.q: For which patient is cromolyn a reasonable prophylactic choice per Heuer?
o: A child 2 years old or younger
q.e: Heuer pairs prophylaxis in patients ≤ 2 years with montelukast or cromolyn. Safer, though less potent, than steroids.

q.q: What are the typical side effects of cromolyn?
o: Mild local cough and throat irritation
q.e: Mild, local and poorly absorbed — why it is used in toddlers.

q.q: What does a Levy-Jennings chart plot?
o: Control results over time vs the mean and ±2 SD
Patient ABG results over a hospital stay
q.e: A record of standard (control) sample measurements used to statistically evaluate analyzer performance.

q.q: What are the usual control limits on a Levy-Jennings chart?
q.e: Values inside ±2 SD = in control. A value outside ±2 SD indicates an analytical error.

q.q: A single control value falls outside ±2 SD, and the next values return to normal. What type of error is this?
q.e: Random error: an isolated point. Reanalyze after two-point calibration; if back in control, no further action.

q.q: Control values drift progressively upward over successive runs. What is this called?
q.e: A trend = gradual deterioration (aging electrode, degrading buffer). It is a bias error.

q.q: Control values jump abruptly to a new level and stay there. What is this called?
q.e: A shift = abrupt change (new reagent lot, replaced electrode, new gas cylinder). Also a bias error.

q.q: The Levy-Jennings chart shows a systematic (bias) error. What must happen?
o: Stop patient testing until it is fixed
Continue testing and note the error
Rerun the control once and continue
Widen the control limits to ±3 SD
q.e: Bias is always serious. Troubleshoot, repair or replace, recalibrate, and confirm controls before resuming.

q.q: How many levels of control media must be run for blood gas analyzer calibration verification?
q.e: At least 3 levels (acidotic, normal, alkalotic) spanning the reportable range, at least daily and after maintenance.

q.q: What is the gold standard for verifying PO₂ and PCO₂ on a blood gas analyzer?
q.e: Tonometry equilibrates a liquid medium to a reference gas of known partial pressures.

q.q: Per the deck's Westgard framing, two or more consecutive controls outside the acceptable range indicate:
o: Out of control — recalibrate or replace
q.e: One control outside = warning; two or more consecutive outside = out of control.

q.q: In proficiency testing, who provides the samples?
o: An outside agency sends blind samples
The RT draws a sample from a healthy volunteer
q.e: The agency compares the lab's results to its own and to peer labs. Certification is needed for Medicare/Medicaid reimbursement.

q.q: What is a point-of-care analyzer?
o: A device that runs lab tests at the bedside
A bench analyzer in the central lab
A pulse oximeter with a finger probe
q.e: POCT: collection, measurement and reporting at or near the site of care. Most use disposable, self-calibrating cartridges.

q.q: Which is an example of a point-of-care analyzer?
q.e: The i-STAT returns ABG results in about 90 seconds and can run electrolytes, Hb, glucose, lactate and BUN.

q.q: How soon must an i-STAT sample be analyzed, and should it be iced?
o: Within 3 minutes; do NOT ice it
Within 10 minutes; do not ice it
q.e: i-STAT: analyze within 3 minutes, not on ice.

q.q: What is the best way to validate POCT measurements?
o: Run the same sample on a bench analyzer too
Run the same cartridge a second time
Compare with the pulse oximeter reading
q.e: Inter-instrumental comparison is Heuer's T4 tip.

q.q: A POCT device fails to calibrate twice with new cartridges. What should the RT do?
o: Take it out of service; use another or the lab
Keep trying new cartridges until it passes
Report the results with a comment
Calibrate it manually with room air
q.e: Rerun once with a new cartridge; if it fails again, take it out of service.

q.q: A POCT PO₂ is below 40 torr in a patient showing signs of severe hypoxemia. What should the RT do?
o: Increase the FiO₂ now and confirm later
Wait for a central lab repeat before acting
Ignore it as a cartridge error
Repeat the test three times first
q.e: Never wait for a repeat when findings are life-threatening and match the patient's condition.

q.q: How is QC performed on a pulse oximeter?
o: Check it on a healthy person (pulse, 97–100%, signal loss)
Calibrate it with 100% O₂ and then room air
Run three levels of liquid control solution
Compare it against a capnograph reading
q.e: Oximeters measure relative light intensity, so they get operational verification using a "biological control."

q.q: On a healthy subject, a pulse oximeter reads 93%. What should the RT do?
o: Move the probe to the ear and accept any value
q.e: Failure criteria: wrong pulse rate, SpO₂ < 97% on a healthy subject, or failure to detect loss of signal.

q.q: How accurate is a pulse oximeter with good perfusion?
q.e: Relatively accurate (±2–4%) with good perfusion.

q.q: How does carbon monoxide poisoning affect a standard pulse oximeter reading?
q.e: Two-wavelength oximeters read COHb as oxygenated Hb. Use a CO-oximeter.

q.q: What is the MOST common source of pulse oximeter errors and false alarms?
q.e: Motion artifact — relocate the sensor.

q.q: A patient wearing dark nail polish has an SpO₂ reading. What effect does the polish have?
q.e: Dark pigmentation and nail polish read falsely high. Remove polish or rotate the probe 90° in an emergency.

q.q: A patient given methylene blue has a pulse oximeter reading. What effect does the dye have?
q.e: Vascular dyes cause falsely low readings — correlate with an arterial SaO₂.

q.q: A probe fitted too tightly causes venous pulsation. What happens to the SpO₂?
q.e: Venous pooling/pulsation → falsely low SpO₂.

q.q: Before believing an SpO₂ reading, what should the RT check?
o: Its pulse rate matches the actual pulse
The probe is on the index finger
q.e: Make sure the oximeter is actually seeing the patient's pulse.

q.q: What are the two calibration points for an oxygen analyzer?
q.e: Expose to 100%, adjust to 100%, then confirm 21% (±2%) in room air.

q.q: How accurate are polarographic and galvanic oxygen analyzers?
q.e: Both are generally accurate to within ±2%.

q.q: An oxygen analyzer fails its two-point calibration. What does Heuer's T4 tip recommend?
o: Use it anyway and note the error
q.e: Failure to reach 100% or 21% suggests a damaged probe or defective analyzer. Also check for condensate on the membrane.

q.q: An oxygen analyzer reads 0%. What are the likely causes?
o: Too much oxygen flowing past it
q.e: A 0% reading suggests a dead battery, disconnected probe or dead probe.

q.q: Which type of oxygen analyzer requires external power to maintain the electrode reaction?
q.e: Polarographic needs external power; galvanic cells don't (though both need power for alarms).

q.q: What size syringe is used to calibrate a spirometer's volume?
q.e: A large-volume 3.0-L calibration syringe.

q.q: What is the ATS volume accuracy standard for diagnostic spirometers?
q.e: ±3% or ±50 mL. For the 3.0-L syringe, ±3% = 90 mL governs.

q.q: A spirometer is checked with a 3.0-L syringe. What range of readings is acceptable?
How often is spirometer volume calibration checked?
q.e: Leaks and volume: daily. Flow linearity: weekly. Volume linearity and time: quarterly.

q.q: During a spirometer leak test, how much volume loss is allowed?
o: Less than 10 mL in 1 minute at 3 cm H₂O
No more than 3% of the volume
q.e: Pressurize to 3 cm H₂O for 1 minute; the leak must be < 10 mL.

q.q: A 3.0-L syringe calibration reads 3.30 L. What is the most likely cause?
o: The syringe was not fully emptied
The patient did not seal the mouthpiece
q.e: BTPS on makes the calibrating volume read ~10% high. For high readings, also recheck zeroing and temperature.

q.q: A 3.0-L syringe calibration reads 2.80 L. What should the RT do FIRST?
q.e: Low volume → repeat the leak check first. Don't test patients until the cause is found and calibration is accurate.

q.q: How many acceptable FVC maneuvers does the ATS require?
q.e: Get at least three error-free maneuvers.

q.q: What is the ATS repeatability criterion for FVC and FEV₁?
o: The two largest values must be within 150 mL
All values must be within 50 mL
The two largest values must be within 500 mL
The best value must exceed 80% predicted
q.e: The two largest FVC and FEV₁ values must each be within 0.150 L.

q.q: What is the minimum exhalation time for an acceptable FVC maneuver?
q.e: At least 6 seconds (severe COPD may take up to 15).

q.q: An FVC curve has an S-shaped, slow start with a back-extrapolated volume over 150 mL. What is the error, and the coaching cue?
q.e: Back-extrapolated volume ≥ 5% of FVC or 150 mL = unacceptable slow start.

q.q: Which artery is preferred for an ABG, and why?
o: Brachial — larger and easier to feel
q.e: Radial on the nondominant wrist. Brachial, femoral and dorsalis pedis carry greater risk.

q.q: During a modified Allen's test, how quickly should the palm flush after the ulnar artery is released?
q.e: A prolonged delay means inadequate ulnar flow — test the other wrist; if both fail, use the brachial artery.

q.q: How long should pressure be held after an arterial puncture?
o: At least 5 minutes, more if anticoagulated
No pressure is needed after an ABG
q.e: Deck: at least 5 minutes; recheck the site after 20 minutes.

q.q: What must be documented with every ABG sample?
q.e: Always document FiO₂, device, vent mode/settings and related assessments.

q.q: Within what time must an ABG in a plastic syringe at room temperature be analyzed (Heuer)?
q.e: Heuer: < 30 min. Shunt study < 5 min. High WBC/platelets: immediately. > 30 min: glass syringe on ice (0–4°C).

q.q: An ABG sample will not be run for 45 minutes. How should it be stored?
o: In a glass syringe chilled to 0–4°C
In a plastic syringe at room temperature
In a plastic syringe in a warm water bath
q.e: Chilling slows cellular metabolism and preserves the values.

q.q: Which are the three analytical stages of ABG error?
q.e: Preanalytical (before analysis), analytical (during measurement), postanalytical (data handling and reporting).

q.q: An air bubble in the sample is which type of error?
q.e: Heuer's three most common preanalytical errors: air bubbles, venous admixture, continued metabolism.

q.q: A drifting analyzer electrode or contaminated buffer is which type of error?
q.e: Analytical errors happen while the analyzer runs the sample.

q.q: Entering the wrong patient information on the ABG report is which type of error?
q.e: Postanalytical: transcription errors, wrong patient info, failing to record FiO₂.

q.q: How does an air bubble in an ABG sample affect the results?
q.e: CO₂ diffuses into the bubble; PO₂ is pulled toward room air (~150 torr) — falsely high if true PO₂ was lower, falsely low if higher.

q.q: An ABG sample sat at room temperature for 2 hours without ice. How are the results affected?
q.e: Continued metabolism: cells make CO₂ and consume O₂ → falsely acidotic. The opposite of an air bubble on PCO₂ and pH.

q.q: How does venous admixture affect an ABG sample?
q.e: Recognized by no pulsation as the syringe fills and darker blood.

q.q: How does too much heparin in the syringe affect the ABG?
o: No effect on any measured value
PaO₂ falls to zero, pH unchanged
q.e: Heparin dilutes the sample and is acidic, so pH drifts toward 7.0.

q.q: What is a hemoximeter (CO-oximeter)?
o: A multi-wavelength device that measures each Hb type
A two-wavelength pulse oximeter on the finger
An electrode that measures only the PO₂
A heated sensor that estimates PO₂ through skin
q.e: Each Hb species absorbs different wavelengths, so each can be measured directly.

q.q: Which values does a CO-oximeter measure directly?
o: HbO₂, HHb, COHb, MetHb, total Hb
q.e: Plus sulfhemoglobin per Heuer. A blood gas analyzer measures only pH, PCO₂, PO₂ and calculates SaO₂.

q.q: A smoke inhalation victim needs an oxygenation assessment. Which test is required?
q.e: SpO₂ reads falsely high and PaO₂ may be normal in CO poisoning; the ABG SaO₂ is calculated.

q.q: During inhaled nitric oxide therapy, CO-oximetry is used to monitor:
q.e: iNO can cause methemoglobinemia.

q.q: A COHb level of 25% indicates:
q.e: COHb: 1–3% normal; 5–10% smokers; 10–15% heavy smokers; > 20% CO poisoning.

q.q: An SpO₂ disagrees with the lab. What should the SpO₂ be compared against?
q.e: The ABG SaO₂ is usually computed, so compare to a hemoximeter and use the SaO₂ − SpO₂ difference.

q.q: On BiPAP, IPAP mainly affects ______ and EPAP mainly affects ______.
q.e: IPAP → VT/CO₂. EPAP is functionally PEEP → FRC, recruitment, SpO₂.

q.q: What is the minimum difference between IPAP and EPAP per the decks?
q.e: ΔP (pressure support) = IPAP − EPAP, never less than 4 cm H₂O.

q.q: Which BiPAP adjustment rule is most often tested?
o: Never raise EPAP without raising IPAP equally
Never raise IPAP without raising EPAP equally
Always lower IPAP and EPAP together
Raise EPAP by itself to lower the CO₂
q.e: Raising EPAP alone shrinks ΔP and costs ventilation. Heuer: to avoid changing PaCO₂, keep ΔP constant.

q.q: A patient on BiPAP 10/5 needs better OXYGENATION only. Which change is correct?
q.e: Raise both equally: ΔP stays 5, baseline rises.

q.q: A patient on BiPAP 10/5 needs better VENTILATION only. Which change is correct?
q.e: Raise IPAP only: ΔP 5 → 10, baseline unchanged. (If oxygenation is stable, lowering EPAP also widens ΔP.)

q.q: A patient on BiPAP 10/5 needs better oxygenation AND ventilation. Which change is correct?
q.e: Raise both, IPAP more: ΔP 5 → 8 and baseline rises.

q.q: A COPD patient on BiPAP has pH 7.28 and PaCO₂ 75 mm Hg. What should be adjusted?
q.e: A ventilation problem → raise IPAP (ΔP).

q.q: A CHF patient on BiPAP has SpO₂ 84% with a normal PaCO₂. What should be adjusted?
q.e: An oxygenation problem → raise EPAP, keeping ΔP constant.

q.q: Why does Heuer keep IPAP below 20–25 cm H₂O?
o: It opens the esophagus and inflates the stomach
q.e: 20–25 cm H₂O is the esophageal opening pressure — gastric insufflation risk.

q.q: Which is a contraindication to BiPAP?
q.e: Also: respiratory or cardiac arrest, can't protect airway or clear secretions, facial trauma, vomiting, obtundation.

q.q: Which is a hazard of BiPAP?
q.e: Hazards: aerophagia, gastric insufflation, dryness, aspiration, claustrophobia, ↓ cardiac output, eye irritation, pressure sores.

q.q: Per Heuer, which finding indicates BiPAP failure requiring intubation?
o: Worsening ABGs in the first 1–2 hours
q.e: Heuer: worsening ABGs in 1–2 hr, no improvement after 4 hr, pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ > 60, P/F < 200, or RR > 35. (Decks: still deteriorating at 30 minutes.)

q.q: Which interface is preferred when starting NPPV for ACUTE respiratory failure?
q.e: Lower leak. Avoid it if vomiting/aspiration risk is high. For chronic hypercapnia, nasal devices (less deadspace).

q.q: A patient on a nasal BiPAP mask is leaking through the mouth. What is the fix?
q.e: Mouth leak → chin strap (Heuer Table 6-24).

q.q: Which interface is used for CPAP but is not recommended for BiPAP?
q.e: Pillows are smallest and most comfortable but cause congestion, dry mouth and nosebleeds.

q.q: What initial CPAP does Heuer recommend for acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
q.e: Heuer: start at 10 and 100%, titrate to SpO₂ > 90%. Decks: CPAP 8–12 with 100%.

q.q: In volume control, how is the tidal volume achieved?
o: A set VT; pressure varies with the lungs
A set pressure; the VT varies
The backup rate sets the VT
q.e: Only one of volume or pressure can be controlled; the other varies.

q.q: In PSV, what determines the tidal volume?
o: A preset volume on the ventilator
q.e: The same PS 10 might give 700 mL in good lungs and 300 mL in ARDS.

q.q: When should a patient be switched from VC to PC per Heuer?
q.e: Switch VC → PC when Pplat > 30, using a pressure limit ≤ 30.

q.q: On A/C, the rate is set at 12 and the patient triggers 24 breaths/min. How many full breaths are delivered?
q.e: Every breath, assisted or controlled, gets the full preset breath.

q.q: On SIMV, how is the VT of a spontaneous breath determined?
o: The patient's effort, plus any PS
q.e: Mandatory breaths get the set VT; spontaneous breaths are whatever the patient generates.

q.q: On SIMV at a rate of 10, how often is a mandatory breath delivered?
q.e: 60 ÷ 10 = 6 seconds per mandatory breath.

q.q: A patient on A/C is hyperventilating because of a high trigger rate. What does Heuer recommend?
q.e: SIMV is indicated when full support is needed but the patient's rate causes hyperventilation on A/C.

q.q: How does PSV end inspiration?
o: When flow falls to ~25% of peak
When a set volume is delivered
When a set time has elapsed
When pressure hits the alarm limit
q.e: PSV = patient-triggered, pressure-limited, flow-cycled.

q.q: What is PRVC's main advantage?
o: A guaranteed VT at the lowest possible pressure
It works on apneic patients without a rate
q.e: PRVC adjusts pressure breath to breath. Disadvantage: when patient demand rises, pressure may drop just when support is needed.

q.q: Which statement about CPAP is correct?
o: It oxygenates but does not ventilate
It is best for apneic patients
q.e: CPAP is wrong for the apneic, oversedated or severely fatigued patient.

q.q: Which patient benefits most from APRV?
o: ALI with Pplat > 30 or refractory hypoxemia
A COPD patient with severe air trapping
A patient ready for extubation today
q.e: APRV needs a patient who can breathe spontaneously; auto-PEEP is usually present and desired.

q.q: What is Heuer's initial VT for full ventilatory support?
o: 12 mL/kg IBW with no Pplat limit
q.e: 4–6 mL/kg in ARDS.

q.q: What is the first step when any ventilator alarm sounds?
q.e: Alarm → patient → ventilator → cause → fix. Never silence without finding the cause.

q.q: Where is the high pressure alarm set per the decks?
q.e: Heuer also allows 50 cm H₂O. It must not be raised without justification.

q.q: The low exhaled VT and low pressure alarms sound together. What is the problem?
q.e: Low volume + LOW pressure = leak. Low volume + HIGH pressure = obstruction.

q.q: The low exhaled VT and high pressure alarms sound together. What is the problem?
q.e: Find it: drain condensate, replace the HME, suction. An expiratory obstruction is the more dangerous kind.

q.q: What is the apnea alarm delay per Heuer?
q.e: Heuer 20 seconds; decks 15–20 seconds.

q.q: The high FiO₂ alarm suddenly sounds. Which is a likely cause?
o: A leak in the patient circuit
q.e: Also gas source failure or analyzer needing calibration.

q.q: PIP rose from 30 to 45 cm H₂O; Pplat is unchanged at 25. What is the likely cause?
q.e: High PIP with normal Pplat = resistance. "When only PIP moves, think airways."

q.q: PIP and Pplat both rise suddenly by 15 cm H₂O and breath sounds disappear on one side. What should the RT suspect?
o: A leak in the ventilator circuit
A mucus plug partly blocking the ETT
q.e: Compliance problem. Sudden = search for the problem; gradual (pneumonia, ARDS) = treat the disease.

q.q: Which circuit is used on most critical care ventilators?
q.e: The expiratory limb returns gas to the ventilator, allowing accurate exhaled-volume measurement.

q.q: Which circuit is typical for home-care and transport ventilators?
q.e: A pneumatic line closes the valve on inspiration; it can also provide PEEP.

q.q: Which circuit is used for noninvasive (NPPV) ventilators?
q.e: Continuous flow flushes exhaled gas out the port — why EPAP must never fall near zero.

q.q: How does high circuit compliance affect the delivered VT?
o: It lowers the VT reaching the patient
It raises the VT reaching the patient
It has no effect on the VT
q.e: At PIP 40, a 5 mL/cm H₂O circuit holds 200 mL; a 3 mL/cm H₂O circuit holds 120 mL.

q.q: How much water vapor must gas reaching the airway of an intubated patient carry?
q.e: Heuer: ≥ 30 mg/L via heated humidifier or HME.

q.q: What temperature range does Heuer give for a heated humidifier?
q.e: Decks target 37°C. 30–31°C at 70–90% RH describes an HME.

q.q: Which patient is the WORST candidate for an HME?
o: A patient with thick, bloody secretions
A stable patient going to CT
A patient with thin, scant secretions
q.e: Also avoid with NPPV, ARDS on low VT, hypercapnic failure, high VE, hypothermia, large leaks.

q.q: Where is an HME placed?
o: Between the wye and the artificial airway
On the inspiratory limb at the ventilator
q.e: It always adds deadspace and must allow bidirectional flow.

q.q: What is the most common threat to ventilator circuit patency?
q.e: Fix with heated-wire circuits, inline water traps at low points, or an HME.

q.q: What does hyperventilation cause?
q.e: Classic ABG: pH 7.52, PaCO₂ 30, HCO₃⁻ 24.

q.q: How does hyperventilation affect cerebral blood flow and ICP?
o: No effect on the brain at all
q.e: CO₂ is a potent cerebral vasodilator; lowering it constricts cerebral arterioles.

q.q: Why does Heuer say to avoid routine hyperventilation in head injury?
o: It lowers ICP but risks ischemia
q.e: Reserve it for pre-suctioning spikes, confirmed herniation, or salvage therapy.

q.q: What PaCO₂ does Heuer target for a TBI patient?
q.e: Also PIP ≤ 30, SpO₂ > 95%, avoid high PEEP.

q.q: Prolonged respiratory alkalosis (> 24 hours) shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve which way?
q.e: "Left = Love." Tissues, especially the brain, don't get O₂ efficiently.

q.q: A patient on VC SIMV (rate 14, VT 6–7 mL/kg) has a low PaCO₂ and PaO₂ 115 on 40%. What should be changed?
q.e: Heuer's NBRC item: VT is already appropriate — the problem is ventilation.

q.q: A weaning patient is hyperventilating because of anxiety and hypoxemia. What should the RT do?
o: Find and fix the cause before reducing support
Cut ventilator support to normalize the PaCO₂
q.e: Cutting support worsens hyperventilation, fatigues the muscles and causes ventilatory failure.

q.q: What is the BEST predictor of weaning success?
o: A clear chest x-ray on the day of weaning
A PaO₂ above 100 mm Hg on any FiO₂
q.e: "We don't wean the ventilator — we wean the patient." No single value determines readiness.

q.q: Which oxygenation criteria must be met to begin a weaning assessment?
q.e: Plus reversal of the cause, pH ≥ 7.25, hemodynamic stability, and inspiratory effort.

q.q: How is the rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI) calculated?
q.e: RSBI = f ÷ VT(L). Measure off the ventilator for about 3 minutes.

q.q: A patient breathes spontaneously at 38/min with a VT of 300 mL. What is the RSBI, and what does it predict?
A patient breathes at 20/min with a VT of 500 mL. What is the RSBI?
q.e: 20 ÷ 0.5 = 40. < 105 is favorable (< 50 normal).

q.q: Above what RSBI value does weaning failure become likely?
q.e: RSBI > 105 predicts failure. RR and RSBI are the best indicators of tolerance of spontaneous breathing.

q.q: A MIP/NIF of −15 cm H₂O indicates:
q.e: Critical: weaker than −20 to −25 cm H₂O. Normal −80 to −100. More negative = stronger.

q.q: How long is a NIF/MIP maneuver held against the one-way valve?
q.e: The patient "bucks down" toward RV; maximal effort is ensured and consciousness is not required.

q.q: What spontaneous VT is critically low for weaning (Heuer)?
q.e: Normal 5–7 mL/kg PBW.

q.q: What vital capacity is critically low for weaning (Heuer)?
q.e: Normal ~70 mL/kg (Heuer) or 50 mL/kg (decks).

q.q: What minute ventilation is associated with poor weaning outcomes?
q.e: Critical < 4 or > 10 L/min.

q.q: How long should a spontaneous breathing trial last once the screening period is passed?
q.e: Most failures occur within the first 20–30 minutes.

q.q: Which SBT methods are acceptable?
o: T-tube, CPAP, PS 5–8, or CPAP + PS
SIMV at a rate of 10 only
q.e: No method is better than another. SIMV is not recommended as a stand-alone weaning mode.

q.q: During an SBT, which finding indicates failure?
q.e: Pass: SpO₂ ≥ 85–90%, pH ≥ 7.30, PaCO₂ rise ≤ 10, HR < 120–140 (< 20% change), RR ≤ 30–35 (< 50% change).

q.q: A patient fails an SBT. What happens next?
o: Full support, fix the cause, retry in 24 hr
Extubate anyway and watch very closely
Repeat the same SBT again in 1 hour
Switch to gradual SIMV weaning instead
q.e: Repeat the SBT every 24 hours.

q.q: What does a POSITIVE qualitative cuff-leak test indicate?
o: A leak around the cuff — airway likely patent
No leak — high risk of post-extubation stridor
The cuff balloon is damaged and must be replaced
The patient is ready for a tracheostomy
q.e: Heuer: deflate the cuff, occlude the tube; leakage during breathing = positive.

q.q: What MEP or peak cough flow indicates adequate secretion clearance before extubation?
o: MEP > 60 cm H₂O or peak cough flow > 60 L/min
q.e: Heuer's extubation thresholds for an alert patient.

q.q: Stridor develops right after extubation. What should the RT recommend?
o: Cool humidified O₂ and racemic epinephrine
Lower the FiO₂ to reduce swelling
q.e: Keep racemic epinephrine available at extubation.

q.q: A patient has a high PaCO₂ on the ventilator. Which setting should be changed?
q.e: CO₂ problem → ventilation; O₂ problem → FiO₂/PEEP. FiO₂ does not lower PaCO₂.

q.q: When changing ventilation, which setting is usually adjusted FIRST?
q.e: Rate first (8–24/min); VT second (4–8 mL/kg, Pplat ≤ 30).

q.q: A patient on rate 14 has a PaCO₂ of 60 mm Hg. The target is 40. What new rate is needed?
A patient on rate 12 has a PaCO₂ of 50 mm Hg. The target is 40. What new rate is needed?
A patient has VE 6.0 L/min and PaCO₂ 55 mm Hg. The target PaCO₂ is 40. What minute ventilation is needed?
VT is 450 mL with PaCO₂ 58 mm Hg; the target is 45. The rate is already near maximum. What VT is needed?
q.e: (450 × 58) ÷ 45 = 580 mL — then check Pplat ≤ 30.

q.q: PaO₂ is 70 torr on FiO₂ 0.40. How should oxygenation be improved per the 60-60 rule?
q.e: PaO₂ > 60 on FiO₂ < 0.6 = V/Q → FiO₂. PaO₂ < 60 on FiO₂ > 0.6 = shunt → PEEP.

q.q: PaO₂ is 52 torr on FiO₂ 0.80. What should be increased?
q.e: Shunt → add or increase PEEP/CPAP.

q.q: When weaning oxygen support, what should be reduced FIRST?
q.e: Drop FiO₂ to ≤ 0.50 first, then lower PEEP.

q.q: A ventilated patient has a primary metabolic acidosis from DKA. How should the ventilator be managed?
o: Treat the cause; don't compensate with the vent
Raise the rate to normalize the pH
Lower the rate to raise the PaCO₂
Add PEEP to improve the acidosis
q.e: Do not adjust the ventilator for metabolic problems.

q.q: How is STATIC compliance calculated?
q.e: Static uses plateau (no flow, no resistance). Dynamic uses PIP.

q.q: How is DYNAMIC compliance calculated?
q.e: Cdyn includes resistance, so it is always less than Cstat in VC.

q.q: VT 700 mL, PIP 42, Pplat 35, PEEP 8. What is the static compliance?
q.e: 700 ÷ (35 − 8) = 25.9 ≈ 26 (the PIP is a decoy).

q.q: VT 500 mL, PIP 30, Pplat 25, PEEP 5. What is the dynamic compliance?
VT 400 mL, flow 75 L/min, PIP 45, Pplat 30. What is the airway resistance?
What is the normal static compliance for an INTUBATED adult per Heuer and the 203 deck?
q.e: RCP 105 decks: 60–100. Below 25–30 = ↑ WOB and weaning difficulty; > 30 is the weaning minimum.

q.q: How is Pplat read from a pressure–time curve?
o: Add an end-inspiratory pause; read the flat shelf
Read the highest point of the pressure curve
Average the pressure over the whole breath
q.e: Heuer: 0.5–2.0 sec pause during volume ventilation with square flow.

q.q: During an inspiratory pause, the patient exhales and the plateau rises erratically. What is the effect?
q.e: Exhaling during the pause → falsely high; inhaling → falsely low.

q.q: A true descending-ramp breath delivers 1 L/sec for 0.5 sec with PIP 35 cm H₂O (flow reaches zero). What is the compliance?
q.e: VT = 1 × 0.5 = 500 mL. Flow zero → PIP = Pplat. 500 ÷ 35 = 14.3.

q.q: Over 4 hours, Pplat − PEEP stays constant while PIP − Pplat rises from 20 to 35. What is happening?
q.e: Heuer Box 4-5: pure resistance problem — bronchospasm, secretions, edema, tube occlusion.

q.q: Why is static compliance useful as a weaning parameter?
o: It is independent of patient effort
q.e: Static compliance, Raw and VD/VT are effort-independent.

q.q: Where is the tip of a MACINTOSH (curved) blade placed?
o: In the vallecula, lifting the epiglottis indirectly
Under the epiglottis, lifting it directly
q.e: Miller (straight) goes under the epiglottis and lifts it directly.

q.q: Which ETT sizes should be available at the bedside for intubation?
o: Chosen size, one larger, one smaller
The chosen size and one smaller
q.e: Always have one size larger and one size smaller.

q.q: Which statement about the stylet is correct?
o: Oral only; tip never past the ETT tip
Tip should extend 2 cm past the ETT
q.e: Magill forceps are required for nasal intubation; a stylet is never used nasally.

q.q: How long should each intubation attempt last per Heuer Ch 9?
q.e: ≤ 20 seconds (Ch 16 says ≤ 30), with 1–2 minutes of oxygenation between attempts.

q.q: What position is used for oral intubation?
q.e: Sniffing position, suction the oropharynx, hyperoxygenate 1–2 minutes.

q.q: How far past the vocal cords should the cuff be advanced?
q.e: Advance until the cuff disappears 2–3 cm past the cords, then inflate to 20–30 cm H₂O.

q.q: A colorimetric CO₂ detector confirms tracheal placement when it changes:
q.e: Purple → yellow/tan sustained over ≥ 6 breaths. False negative in cardiac arrest.

q.q: Gurgling is heard over the epigastrium after intubation. What should the RT do?
o: Advance the tube 2 cm and recheck
Pull the tube back 2 cm and recheck
q.e: Epigastric gurgling = esophageal intubation.

q.q: After intubation, breath sounds are decreased on the LEFT. What is the likely cause and fix?
o: Left pneumothorax — insert a chest tube
q.e: The tube is too deep, usually into the right mainstem.

q.q: What are the only two ways to confirm the tube is properly above the carina?
q.e: Breath sounds and CO₂ prove the tube is in the airway, not that its depth is right.

q.q: On chest x-ray, where should the ETT tip sit?
q.e: Read with the head neutral — the tube moves with neck flexion and extension.

q.q: What is the average oral ETT depth at the incisors for an adult male?
q.e: Males 21–23 cm; females 19–21 cm; add 2 cm for nasal.

q.q: A Cormack-Lehane Grade IV view shows:
q.e: Grade III = epiglottis only; Grade IV = no epiglottis.

q.q: Which mnemonic predicts a difficult INTUBATION?
q.e: LEMON: Look, Evaluate, Mallampati, Obesity/Obstruction, Neck mobility. MOANS predicts difficult BVM ventilation.

q.q: How is an OPA sized?
o: Mouth corner to angle of the jaw
Tip of the nose to the earlobe
q.e: 80 mm (3) average adult female, 90 mm (4) average adult male.

q.q: An OPA is appropriate for which patient?
o: A comatose patient whose tongue blocks the airway
An alert patient recovering from surgery
A patient with an intact gag reflex
q.e: Not for conscious patients — gagging, vomiting, aspiration. Remove it immediately if the patient gags.

q.q: A patient with a gag reflex needs an airway adjunct to relieve upper airway obstruction. Which should be used?
q.e: The NPA is the alternative when the gag is intact, or with trismus/seizures preventing mouth opening.

q.q: What size NPA is typical for an average adult male?
q.e: #6 (24 Fr) average female; #7 (28 Fr) average male.

q.q: Which rule applies to NPA use?
o: Never cut an NPA — the cut edge is sharp
Insert it with force if resistance is met
Use it in patients with nasal polyps
q.e: Lubricate with water-soluble jelly; if it won't pass, try the other naris, then a smaller size.

q.q: When is a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) indicated?
o: As a rescue in the "can ventilate, can't intubate" scenario
As a long-term airway for PPV
To prevent aspiration in a full-stomach patient
In a conscious patient with a gag reflex
q.e: The LMA is not a definitive airway and gives no aspiration protection.

q.q: What is the maximum LMA cuff pressure?
q.e: Never exceed 60 cm H₂O. If a leak occurs, reposition — don't just add air.

q.q: What is the main advantage of a tracheostomy tube over an ETT for long-term ventilation?
o: Lower resistance, more comfort, and easier suctioning
It can be placed at the bedside by the RT
q.e: Also less tube movement and easier reinsertion into a mature stoma.

q.q: Why is the obturator kept at the bedside of a trach patient?
o: For reinsertion if the tube comes out
To pass a suction catheter through
q.e: Remove it immediately after insertion (it blocks the airway) and keep it at the bedside.

q.q: What is a tracheostomy button used for?
o: Keeping the stoma open after the trach is removed
Sealing the airway with a cuff
q.e: No ventilatory support and no cuff. Distress with an uncapped button = protruding too far into the trachea.

q.q: In a "can't ventilate, can't intubate" child under 12, what surgical airway does Heuer prefer?
q.e: The small trachea makes cricothyrotomy hazardous. Jet ventilation is temporary, not definitive.

q.q: A tube that is too small for the trachea causes what cuff problem?
o: High cuff pressure needed to seal
A cuff that cannot be inflated
q.e: Fix = exchange for a larger tube, not more air.

q.q: What is the recommended cuff pressure range?
q.e: 30 = maximum; < 20 invites microaspiration and VAP; 25 is the typical NBRC high limit.

q.q: What is normal tracheal capillary perfusion pressure?
q.e: Keep the cuff < 25 mm Hg, and lower still in a hypotensive patient.

q.q: 30 cm H₂O is approximately how many mm Hg?
A leak-free seal cannot be achieved at 30 cm H₂O. What does Heuer recommend?
o: Stay < 25–30 and change to a larger tube
Keep adding air until the leak stops
Switch to the minimal leak technique
q.e: Never just keep adding air.

q.q: Why does Heuer say to avoid the minimal leak technique in ventilated patients?
o: It increases the risk of VAP
It raises cuff pressure too high
q.e: Maintain 20–30 cm H₂O instead. The deck presents MOV and MLT as equal options.

q.q: Why must cuff pressure be ADJUSTED, not just measured, when a manometer is attached?
o: The manometer steals volume and lowers it
q.e: Check at least once per shift and whenever the tube is moved or a leak appears.

q.q: Using the uncuffed formula, what size ETT does a 4-year-old need?
Using the CUFFED formula, what size ETT does a 4-year-old need?
q.e: Cuffed = (age ÷ 4) + 3 → 4.0 mm.

q.q: Using the uncuffed formula, what size ETT does an 8-year-old need?
q.e: (8 ÷ 4) + 4 = 6.0 mm; insertion length 15–17 cm.

q.q: What ETT is used for a premature infant under 3 kg?
q.e: Uncuffed tubes are recommended for premature infants and anyone < 3 kg.

q.q: What ETT size does Heuer give for an adult female?
q.e: Heuer: female 7.0–8.0, male 8.0–9.0 (deck: 7–7.5 and 8–8.5).

q.q: Using Hess's rule, how deep should an ETT be at the lips in a 3-kg neonate?
q.e: Weight in kg + 6 cm = 9 cm.

q.q: What is the purpose of the WATER-SEAL chamber in a chest drainage system?
o: A one-way valve that lets air out, not in
It collects blood and pleural fluid
It sets the amount of suction
q.e: The tube is submerged 2 cm; refill if the level falls below 2 cm.

q.q: What determines the suction applied to the pleural space in a water-filled system?
o: Water depth in the suction-control chamber
The depth of the water seal
q.e: Fill to 20 cm → −20 cm H₂O, whether the wall reads 80 or 150 mm Hg.

q.q: What suction level is usually applied to a chest tube?
q.e: Deck −10 to −20; Heuer usually −20.

q.q: Gentle continuous bubbling is seen in the SUCTION-CONTROL chamber. What does it mean?
q.e: Vigorous bubbling means the wall vacuum is too high — more noise and evaporation, not more suction.

q.q: Continuous bubbling is seen in the WATER-SEAL chamber. What does it indicate?
q.e: Pinch the tube at the insertion site: bubbling stops → leak at site or patient; continues → leak in the system.

q.q: The water-seal chamber shows no tidaling. What does this mean?
o: The suction is set too high
q.e: Check for kinks and dependent loops, milk the tubing; if it fails, assess for pneumothorax.

q.q: How does the water-seal level move during spontaneous breathing?
o: Rises on inspiration, falls on expiration
Falls on inspiration, rises on expiration
q.e: Reversed during positive pressure ventilation.

q.q: Drainage eyelets on the chest tube become visible outside the chest. What should the RT do?
o: Notify the physician; don't push it in
Push the tube back in gently
q.e: The tube has partially pulled out.

q.q: How should a patient with a chest tube be transported?
o: Unit below chest level, tube NOT clamped
q.e: Clamping can convert an air leak into a tension pneumothorax.

q.q: Which direction is a chest tube aimed for a pneumothorax versus a hemothorax?
o: Superiorly for air; inferiorly/posteriorly for fluid
Inferiorly for air; superiorly for fluid
q.e: Air rises, fluid falls.

q.q: Where is needle decompression performed for a tension pneumothorax?
q.e: Then a chest tube at the 4th–5th ICS.

q.q: What are the deck's criteria for chest tube removal?
o: < 100 mL/day, lung up, no air leak
As soon as suction bubbling stops
q.e: Follow up with a CXR in 4 hours; crepitus at the site suggests air leaking back.

q.q: On chest x-ray, which finding suggests a PNEUMOTHORAX?
o: Black space with no lung markings at the edge
Blunted costophrenic angle with a meniscus
Air bronchograms in a white area
q.e: Supine films may show a deep sulcus sign. Exam: hyperresonance, absent breath sounds.

q.q: On chest x-ray, what is the earliest sign of a pleural effusion?
q.e: Also a meniscus; confirm with a lateral decubitus film.

q.q: Which way does the trachea shift with a large pneumothorax or pleural effusion?
q.e: Toward areas of collapse; away from space-occupying processes.

q.q: Which way does the trachea shift with lobar atelectasis?
q.e: Atelectasis also elevates the hemidiaphragm on the affected side.

q.q: White (radiopaque) areas with air bronchograms on chest x-ray indicate:
q.e: ARDS = bilateral diffuse infiltrates; VAP = new or progressive infiltrate.

q.q: A hemothorax is confirmed when the pleural fluid hematocrit is:
q.e: Treat with a large-bore chest tube (about 36 Fr), directed inferiorly.

q.q: How is pleurisy recognized?
o: Friction rub with pain on deep breaths
A distinct white shadow on the CXR
Tracheal shift toward the affected side
q.e: Pleurisy has no distinct CXR appearance of its own unless an effusion develops.

q.q: Which effusion is caused by systemic pressure changes like CHF or cirrhosis?
q.e: Transudate: thin, low-protein, few cells — fix the systemic problem. Exudate: high protein from local disease.

q.q: An effusion with high protein and many cells from pneumonia or cancer is a:
q.e: High protein = local pleural disease. Exudates need antibiotics, drainage or a cancer workup.

q.q: When is therapeutic thoracentesis recommended?
q.e: Diagnostic thoracentesis determines transudate vs exudate.

q.q: Before thoracentesis, what should the RT recommend?
q.e: Coughing during the procedure can injure the lung or pleura.

q.q: After thoracentesis, what imaging is needed?
o: CXR or ultrasound to rule out pneumothorax
No imaging — breath sounds are enough
A CT scan of the head
A V/Q scan of the lungs
q.e: Call the physician for dyspnea, hypotension, chest pain, or hemoptysis.

q.q: How is a recurrent malignant pleural effusion treated long term?
q.e: The sclerosant fuses the pleura; painful pleurisy is the trade-off.

q.q: How is an empyema treated?
o: Drain it — antibiotics alone won't reach pus
Antibiotics alone for two full weeks
Diuretics to pull the fluid off
Observation until it resolves by itself
q.e: Chest tube drainage; may need thoracotomy.
